title: Portrayals of schizophrenia by entertainment media: A content analysis of contemporary movies
screen_reason: Content analysis of 41 English-language theatrical movies (42 characters) released 1990-2010 that feature a main character with schizophrenia, whose stated purpose is 'to ascertain the prevalence of stereotypes and misinformation about schizophrenia'. Two shares of the sampled items carry a specific claim the paper identifies as a myth: 24% stated or implied that traumatic events caused the character's schizophrenia, and 24% contained the myth that love can cure schizophrenia. These are shares of items containing a false claim with a stated denominator, so CONTENT. Both rows are flagged borderline because the items are fictional entertainment rather than informational content, which is a scope call for the adjudicator rather than a coding call.

estimates.definition: The movie stated or implied that traumatic events were responsible for a character's schizophrenia. The paper treats this as false: 'movies have falsely promoted the premise that traumatic life events, such as dysfunctional parenting, cause schizophrenia' and 'Considerable evidence indicates a substantial biological basis for schizophrenia'.
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given. The closest statement is the abstract's: "Critics of entertainment media have indicated that cinematic depictions of schizophrenia are stereotypic and characterized by misinformation about symptoms, causes, and treatment."

estimates.ground_truth_detail: The author coded every movie on a purpose-built checklist and a graduate student trained in the scheme independently coded all movies; disagreements were discussed and resolved. Average agreement across coded variables 89%; Cohen's kappa ranged from .78 (flat affect) to perfect agreement (genius, socioeconomic status). The falsity of the trauma-causation premise is asserted by the author against the psychiatric literature rather than coded item-by-item against a formal external ground truth.
estimates.moderator_quote: English-language commercial movies that featured at least one character with schizophrenia and that were released for theatrical showing between 1990 and 2010 were viewed in their entirety. Sources for locating movies were Internet and print movie databases that allowed a search by topic or keyword. [...] Keyword search terms were "schizophrenia," "mental illness" or "mental problems," "psychiatric illness" or "psychiatric problems," "psychological illness" or "psychological problems," "psychosis," "insanity," "crazy," "hallucinations," and "delusions" or "delusional."
estimates.notes: The full sentence reads 'A majority (N=31, 74%) of movies did not identify any causal factors associated with schizophrenia, although about one-fourth (N=10, 24%) stated or implied that traumatic events were responsible for a character's schizophrenia'; the text file hyphen-breaks 'associated' and 'schizophrenia' across lines, so the quoted span is the clean middle of it. Denominator ambiguity: the text says 'movies' but the percentages match the 42 characters (10/42 = 23.8%, 31/42 = 73.8%) at least as well as the 41 movies (24.4%, 75.6%); both round to the reported 24% and 74%, and 31 + 10 = 41. Recorded as 42 characters from 41 movies. year 2010 is the last year of the release window, not a coding date, which is not reported. Flagged borderline because the items are fictional feature films: the numerator is a false claim about schizophrenia carried by a story, not informational content presented as news or advice, and whether such items belong in a misinformation-prevalence corpus is a scope decision.

estimates.definition: The movie carried the premise that schizophrenia can be cured by the special empathetic understanding of a loving helper. The paper states this is false: 'Although a special empathetic understanding may help in symptom management, the notion of cure through a loving relationship is fiction.'
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given. The closest statement is the abstract's: "Critics of entertainment media have indicated that cinematic depictions of schizophrenia are stereotypic and characterized by misinformation about symptoms, causes, and treatment."
estimates.source_quote: The myth that love can cure schizo- phrenia was found in nearly one- fourth (N=10, 24%) of the movies.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The author coded every movie on a purpose-built checklist and a graduate student trained in the scheme independently coded all movies; disagreements were discussed and resolved. Average agreement across coded variables 89%; Cohen's kappa ranged from .78 (flat affect) to perfect agreement (genius, socioeconomic status). The falsity of the 'love cures schizophrenia' premise is asserted by the author against the clinical literature rather than coded item-by-item against a formal external ground truth.
estimates.moderator_quote: According to movie critics, movies have falsely promoted the premise that traumatic life events, such as dysfunctional parenting, cause schizophrenia (18) and that schizophrenia can be cured by the special empathetic understanding of a loving helper (7,19,20).
estimates.notes: The source_quote reproduces the text file's line-break hyphenation ('schizo- phrenia', 'one- fourth'); the sentence in the printed paper reads 'The myth that love can cure schizophrenia was found in nearly one-fourth (N=10, 24%) of the movies.' Same sample and denominator as the trauma-causation row, and coincidentally the same count (N=10, 24%); the two are different claims, not stricter and broader versions of one another, so definition_variant is false for both. A movie can carry both myths, so the two rows are not mutually exclusive and must not be summed. Flagged borderline for the same scope reason: the items are fictional feature films.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The paper's broadest misinformation statement was NOT extracted: 'Although all of the movies contained misinformation about schizophrenia, in a few movies the misinformation was judged to be inconsequential and did not detract from an overall accurate and compelling portrayal of schizophrenia' (Discussion). Read as a share this is 41/41 = 100%, but no checklist variable 'contains misinformation' exists in the coding scheme, no count is given, and the sentence is an interpretive summary rather than a coded result; entering a 100% content-prevalence point on that basis would be unsafe. Recorded here verbatim so an adjudicator can overrule. (2) Depicted-attribute shares were not extracted as misinformation: violence toward others 83% (N=35), homicidal behaviour 31% (N=13) of violent characters, unpredictable behaviour 71% (N=30), self-harm 69% (N=29), suicide 24% (N=10), bizarre delusions 67%, auditory hallucinations 62%, visual hallucinations 52%, disorganized speech 21%, flat affect 19%, alogia/avolition 5%, genius 17%, paranormal abilities 12%. These count what a character does, not whether an item is false: a wholly accurate portrayal could be coded into every one of them, and the author's misinformation argument for these is aggregate over-representation relative to epidemiological base rates (e.g. 'a majority of characters engaged in self-harm, and 24% committed suicide, a misleading characterization given that suicide rates among individuals with schizophrenia are estimated to range from 10% to 16%'), not item-level falsity. Under the review's QUALITY-vs-CONTENT rule these are not CONTENT rows. (3) Treatment depictions (psychotropic medications 55%) are descriptive and the paper finds them fairly accurate. (4) Demographic profile of characters (79% male, 95% Caucasian) is called 'another source of misinformation' but is again an aggregate representation argument, not an item-level falsity share. (5) No exposure, reach, sharing or concentration data: audience size is discussed only qualitatively.

rob.design: Single-author content analysis. Frame: English-language commercial movies released for theatrical showing 1990-2010 featuring at least one main character with schizophrenia, located by keyword searches (schizophrenia, mental illness, psychosis, insanity, crazy, hallucinations, delusions, etc.) across Internet Movie Database, Turner Classic Movies, Yahoo! Movies, Netflix, Time Out Film Guide, VideoHound and other anthologies; over 70 movies viewed in their entirety, 41 met inclusion criteria, 42 characters coded. Case definition applied DSM-IV-TR criteria, with movies included even where a labelled character did not meet criteria (e.g. Me, Myself & Irene, Donnie Darko). All movies double-coded by the author and a graduate student trained in the scheme; disagreements discussed and resolved; average agreement 89%, Cohen's kappa .78 to 1.00. No sampling probability, no audience weighting, and no independent ground truth beyond the coders' clinical knowledge.
rob.item6_quote: Movies were included in the content analysis if a main character's unusual behavior or affect was attributed to schizophrenia or if a main character met DSM-IV-TR (13) criteria for diagnosis of schizophrenia by displaying at least two symptoms of schizophrenia (or only one if the symptom was a delusion judged as bizarre) and by showing significant distress or impairment in psychosocial functioning.
rob.item10_quote: A majority (N=31, 74%) of movies did not identify any causal factors associated with schizophrenia, although about one-fourth (N=10, 24%) stated or implied that traumatic events were responsible for a character's schizophrenia.
